statement: How long a drug can still be found by a test after it was last taken is known only roughly. In two narrative reviews, the usual detection times are second-hand figures from single small studies, or from textbooks and laboratory web pages, and the one primary study read that watched people stop (cannabis) could not see when many of them would have turned negative. The first review (Verstraete, 2004, a single-author summary with no stated search) puts one 'typical' study in each cell of its tables for blood, urine and oral fluid, mostly a single controlled dose given to volunteers, in many studies at doses the author calls low compared with street doses and in some to only one or two people, measured as far as possible down to the method's limit of detection rather than at screening cutoffs (some rows use cutoffs), with the longest times taken from people who stopped heavy use in prison or on a detoxification ward. From these it summarizes that after a single dose most drugs could be detected in urine for 1.5 to 4 days, in blood for 1 or 2 days and in oral fluid for 5 to 48 hours, and after chronic use in urine for about a week after last use, longer in extreme cases (benzoylecgonine, a breakdown product of cocaine, 22 days after last use in people using cocaine heavily; cannabis up to about 3 months, the longest reports, 93 and 95 days, being called probably exceptional); hair holds drugs longest, depending on its length, with few data on single doses. It calls detection times extremely variable: they depend on the amount, the route, acute or chronic use, the fluid tested, the test's limit or cutoff, the substance sought and differences between people. In one study it cites, urine was last positive after a single controlled dose of methamphetamine at 87 hours on average (46 to 144) at the method's limit of quantification but at 43 hours (22 to 65) at cutoffs of 500 ng/mL methamphetamine and 200 ng/mL amphetamine. After heavy use, times ran longer than the single-dose figures: in a series of 63 men described as dependent on heroin, 88.4% still screened positive for morphine after 1 day and 44.8% after 6 days (the review gives neither the numbers tested each day nor when the days start), and in 18 people housed on a closed research unit, the last positive cocaine screen came on average 81 hours (34 to 162) after the last use they reported. The second review (Moeller et al., 2017, a clinical review for clinicians) gives a table of 'approximate' urine detection times, adapted from the authors' 2008 review, with no cutoff, test, amount or conditions for any value (for example cocaine metabolites 2 to 4 days; heroin, as morphine, 48 hours; amphetamine and methamphetamine 48 hours; diazepam 30 days and lorazepam 3 days; cannabis 3 days after a single use, 5 to 7 days with use 4 times a week, 10 to 15 days with daily use and more than 30 days in a chronic heavy smoker); its nine sources are a 1987 report, a pain-medicine review, a textbook, the 2008 review, two laboratory web pages, a psychiatry textbook chapter, the 2004 review and a pharmacists' newsletter. It adds that a result below the cutoff is reported as negative, which means the level was below the cutoff, not that the drug was absent, and that the heroin-specific breakdown product 6-acetylmorphine shows in urine only up to about 8 hours. In the one primary study read (Goodwin et al., 2008), 60 adults in the USA who reported cannabis dependence or abuse and regular smoking (on average 9.4 joints a week on 10.6 of the last 14 days) lived on a closed research unit under 24-hour medical surveillance with random drug tests for up to 30 days, and every urine sample was screened by immunoassay at the US federal workplace cutoff of 50 ng/mL; days since last use before admission were not reported, so every time runs from admission. The last positive screen came 0 to 29.8 days after admission, on average 4.6, 9.7 and 15.4 days in the groups whose first sample held the least, middling and most THCCOOH, the breakdown product tested for (relative to creatinine: up to 50, 51 to 150 and above 150 ng/mg; 19, 21 and 20 people). These averages are minimums: 13 of the 20 in the highest group were still screening positive on their last day of observation (on average day 19; for 4 of them day 30), and of the 16 people watched for 27 days or more, 6, all in the highest group, were still positive when watching ended (editors' count from Table II). Six of the 60 never screened positive on the unit, and in 43 of the 46 people who had both negative and positive screens a positive came after the first negative (editors' count), the pattern of positive, negative and positive again that the authors describe as levels fall. None of these sources gives the detection time for a particular person, amount or test. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: How long do drugs show up on a drug test? It is known only roughly. Two expert reviews, which are not new studies, give the usual figures: after one use, most drugs showed in urine for about 1.5 to 4 days, in blood for 1 to 2 days and in saliva for up to 2 days, and for longer after heavy use. But each figure comes from one small study, some of only one or two people given a single dose in a lab, or from textbooks and lab websites, and the result depends on the test: in one study, a dose of meth was found in urine for about 87 hours at a lab's lowest limit but 43 hours at a higher cutoff. After heavy use, figures ran longer: among 63 men described as dependent on heroin, 45 in 100 still tested positive for morphine after 6 days. In the one study that watched people stop, 60 regular cannabis smokers lived on a locked research ward for up to 30 days, counted from when they arrived, not from their last use. Their last positive came anywhere from day 0 to day 30; 13 of the 20 with the highest levels were still positive when watching ended, so the study's averages of about 5 to 15 days undercount, and positives often came back after a negative. A negative result only means the level was below the test's cutoff.
population: People tested for drugs after use: in the studies summarized second-hand by two narrative reviews, mostly healthy volunteers given a single controlled dose (some studies of one or two people) and people who stopped regular use in prison, on a detoxification ward or on a closed research unit; in the one primary study read, 60 adults aged 18 to 45 in the USA (46 men, 14 women; 50 African American; mean age 26.9) who reported cannabis dependence or abuse (DSM-IV terms) and smoking on average 9.4 joints a week on 10.6 of the last 14 days, kept abstinent on a closed research unit
exposure: Last use of a drug, as a single controlled dose given by researchers or as the end of regular use (in prison, on a detoxification ward or on admission to a closed research unit), followed by tests of urine, blood, oral fluid or hair; in the primary study, cannabis smoked before admission (amounts and THC content unknown; days since last use not reported), then enforced abstinence for up to 30 days
comparator: None: detection times are described, not compared with a control group; in some reviewed studies the same samples were read at different limits or cutoffs; in the primary study, groups formed by the THCCOOH/creatinine of the first urine sample

risk_of_bias.note: The reviews' figures cannot be appraised: one author chose one study per cell with no stated search (card sc_verstraete_2004: high), and the clinical review's table comes from textbooks, laboratory web pages, a newsletter and older reviews (card sc_moeller_2017: high). In the primary study (card sc_goodwin_2008: JBI moderate), times run from admission rather than last use, and the last positive is cut off by the end of observation in 22 of the 54 people who ever screened positive; the statement words the averages as minimums, but the true times cannot be recovered, and the paper has internal inconsistencies (an impossible row; 4.3 against 4.6 days; a lowest group said to be all negative by eight days that includes one person positive at 21.8 days).

inconsistency.note: Figures differ widely between studies, drugs, fluids and cutoffs, but the differences follow the conditions the statement gives (single dose against heavy use, detection limit against cutoff, length of follow-up), and the direction agrees: days after a single dose, longer after heavy use, longest for cannabis.

indirectness.note: The question is how long drugs show on the tests people meet. The typical figures come from single, often low, controlled doses in a few volunteers, measured at laboratory detection limits (which give longer times than a screening cutoff, as the methamphetamine example shows) or at assorted cutoffs, and the clinical review's values carry no conditions at all. The primary study used one screening cutoff (50 ng/mL), counted from admission, and studied one selected US sample (77% men, 83% African American, paid, reporting dependence or abuse).

imprecision.note: Each table entry rests on one study, some of one or two people; the heroin percentages come without the numbers tested each day; in the primary study only 16 people were watched for 27 days or more, so the late part of the picture rests on few people.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for narrative reviews or a single case series.

large_effect.note: A descriptive claim is not upgraded for a large effect (METHODS §6.3).

dose_response.note: In the primary study, later last positives went with higher first-sample levels, but the groups were formed by that level and the fits are lines through three group means; not used.

grade.reasoning: Detection times are rated as descriptions (METHODS §6.3): the controlled-dose studies behind the reviews have no comparison group, and the primary study is a case series; start low. Risk of bias −1, indirectness −1 and imprecision −1 (see the domain notes) take it to very low, the floor. The figures from the two narrative reviews are second-hand and the statement says so; the 2004 review reports the numbers of the primary studies it summarizes, which is the only way they are seen here. The one primary study read (Goodwin et al., 2008) is the strongest evidence for cannabis because abstinence was enforced, so later positive screens reflect what was left in the body, not new use; but it cannot give detection times from last use, and its averages are minimums. statement: Some medicines, their breakdown products and a few foods and other products have been reported to make particular urine drug screens read positive when the drug screened for was absent, as described second-hand in two narrative reviews: a review by laboratory-medicine authors of reports published from 2000 on, with a stated search that found 173 articles, 62 of them with data on false positives (Saitman et al., 2014), and a clinical review for clinicians (Moeller et al., 2017). Screens are immunoassays: they use antibodies, which can also bind other substances, including ones whose structure looks unlike the target, and breakdown products. Each report concerns particular tests, and the same medicine often left other tests unaffected; most reports are single case reports, reviews of patients' charts, or experiments adding a medicine to drug-free urine, and some concern tests that have since changed. Examples with counts: in a blinded study, one point-of-care benzodiazepine test was positive in 46 of 50 people taking the HIV medicine efavirenz and negative in 47 of 50 not taking it, while two other point-of-care tests and LC-MS/MS were negative on all the positives; efavirenz also gave false-positive cannabis screens through a breakdown product on three immunoassays, and in another study one brand of test strips was positive in 28 of 30 people taking it while another device and two laboratory assays were negative; and one laboratory amphetamine assay was negative in 6 healthy men before two doses of the antibiotic ofloxacin and positive in all 6 after. By screen, the reviews name, among others: for amphetamine screens, which the clinical review calls the screens most often linked to false positives, pseudoephedrine and ephedrine, bupropion, labetalol, ranitidine, metformin, the supplement DMAA and trazodone (through its breakdown product, on one ecstasy screen and one amphetamine screen but not another), in a table of 33 entries (among them phentermine, methylphenidate and atomoxetine) that mixes false positives with true ones such as prescribed dextroamphetamine and names no tests or frequencies; for benzodiazepine screens, sertraline, efavirenz and oxaprozin; for cannabis screens, efavirenz, NSAID painkillers (2 false positives in 510 samples in one study, called rare), proton pump inhibitors (one case report and a package insert) and, in newborns' urine, several baby wash products at a 20 ng/mL cutoff; for opiate screens, quinolone antibiotics, rifampicin, naloxone added to urine at high concentrations, and poppy seeds (the US federal workplace cutoff for morphine was raised from 300 to 2,000 ng/mL in 1998 to limit positives from poppy seeds and prescribed opiates); for PCP screens, venlafaxine, dextromethorphan, diphenhydramine and tramadol (in case reports, after overdose), the laboratory review adding that a positive PCP screen is rarely a true positive because PCP use is rare and the tests are not specific; for methadone screens, quetiapine, verapamil, diphenhydramine and doxylamine; and for buprenorphine screens, morphine and other opioids added to urine, so that heroin use could make a buprenorphine screen read positive. Only a few frequencies are printed, and none is the chance that a person taking a medicine will screen positive: in one chart review, 41% of amphetamine screens that GC-MS did not confirm (53 patients; the total is not printed) came from people taking bupropion, with no experiment showing that bupropion caused it; in another, 26.5% of benzodiazepine screens that confirmation did not support (26 samples) were linked to sertraline, again without such an experiment (the clinical review gives 27% to 32% from two chart reviews without saying of what); and in a US Department of Defense analysis the supplement DMAA was found in 92.3% of false-positive amphetamine samples. Some medicines give true positives because they are, or turn into, the substance tested for: prescribed amphetamines and lisdexamfetamine on amphetamine screens; dronabinol, a prescribed form of THC, on cannabis screens, which confirmation cannot tell from cannabis; and codeine, which the body turns partly into morphine. Cocaine screens cross-react little: the clinical review finds no evidence for the claim that amoxicillin makes them positive (four immunoassays tested showed none) and says that numbing medicines such as lidocaine, benzocaine, procaine and tetracaine do not, whereas cocaine used as a medical anaesthetic gives true positives and coca leaf tea can make cocaine screens positive. Alcohol tests for ethyl glucuronide can turn positive after hand sanitizer or mouthwash. Both reviews say a screen is presumptive and should be confirmed by a different method, such as GC-MS or LC-MS/MS, which identifies the substance: the clinical review advises always confirming before legal, employment or other decisions with serious consequences, and the laboratory review notes that such testing is limited or absent in many hospital laboratories and takes days, so decisions are often made on unconfirmed screens. The reviews disagree on one test: the clinical review says efavirenz affects the Drug Screen Multi 5 benzodiazepine test, citing the blinded study and another, while the laboratory review reports that test as negative on the efavirenz positives in the blinded study. The laboratory review also says, without data, that in most cases the cause of a false-positive screen is unknown. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Can medicines cause a false positive on a drug test? Yes, some can, on particular tests, according to two expert reviews, which are not new studies. Quick urine screens use antibodies that can react to look-alike molecules. On one benzodiazepine test, 46 of 50 people taking the HIV medicine efavirenz screened positive, although a different lab method found no benzodiazepine and two other quick tests stayed negative. The reviews list, among others, sertraline on benzodiazepine screens; bupropion, pseudoephedrine, labetalol and some others on amphetamine screens; some antibiotics on opiate screens; and venlafaxine, dextromethorphan and tramadol on PCP screens. Most of these come from single case reports or lab experiments with one test. Only a few rough figures exist, and none says how often people taking a medicine screen positive: in one review of patients' charts, 41 in 100 amphetamine screens that a second method did not confirm came from people taking bupropion; in another, about 27 in 100 false benzodiazepine screens were linked to sertraline. Some medicines give true positives because they are, or become, the drug tested for, such as prescribed amphetamines, prescribed THC (dronabinol) and codeine, which the body partly turns into morphine. There is no evidence that amoxicillin makes cocaine tests positive, and numbing medicines such as lidocaine do not. Both reviews say a screen should be checked by a different lab method before decisions with serious consequences.
population: People whose urine was screened for drugs while taking medicines, or after eating or using products, that might react with the screen, as described second-hand in two narrative reviews of published case reports, chart reviews and dosing studies, and of laboratory experiments adding medicines to drug-free urine (reports published from 2000 on in one review; literature from 1946 to 2016 in the other)
exposure: Medicines and their breakdown products (among them efavirenz, sertraline, bupropion, labetalol, pseudoephedrine, trazodone, quinolone antibiotics, rifampicin, venlafaxine, tramadol, dextromethorphan, diphenhydramine, quetiapine and NSAIDs), a supplement (DMAA), foods (poppy seeds, coca leaf tea) and products (baby wash, hand sanitizer, mouthwash) in urine tested with named screening immunoassays
comparator: Confirmation by a different method (GC-MS, LC-MS/MS or another chromatographic method) showing the target drug absent; drug-free urine before a medicine was added; urine before dosing; in one blinded study, people not taking the medicine
outcome: False-positive screening results (a positive immunoassay screen without the target drug) on named tests, the concentration at which they occurred where tested, and how often, where printed; true positives from medicines that are, or become, the substance tested for

evidence.locator: Abstract; Introduction, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Materials and methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Review of false-positive interferences with urine drug-screen immunoassays by laboratory-medicine authors (University of California, San Diego; Samsung Medical Center, Seoul). SciFinder (MEDLINE and CAPLUS) was searched with 'false positive [drug] urine' for amphetamines, tricyclic antidepressants, benzodiazepines, cannabinoids and opiates, a miscellaneous class and over 60 common medicines and illicit drugs, in English, for articles published after 2000: 173 articles, of which 62 held data on false-positive results; older articles were used to clarify. False negatives are not covered. The authors rank evidence from weakest (exposure to the suspected medicine stated, or two-dimensional structures compared) to stronger (a pure standard added at several concentrations to drug-free urine), with chart reviews and measurement in patients' specimens as supportive, and dosing studies with confirmation also used. The introduction says mass-spectrometry testing is limited or absent in many hospital laboratories and its results usually take several days, so care decisions are often made on presumptive positives; that patients with false positives may lose eligibility in rehabilitation programmes or their jobs; and, without data, that in most cases the cause of a false-positive screen is unknown.

risk_of_bias.note: Seen only through two narrative reviews (cards sc_saitman_2014: some concerns; sc_moeller_2017: high). The laboratory review states its search but used one string per drug on one platform, without duplicate screening, and a search for 'false positive' finds reports of interference rather than of tests that did not react; the clinical review's selection is unsystematic, and its Table 4 mixes true and false positives without tests, concentrations or frequencies. The reports themselves are mostly single case reports, chart reviews without experiments (bupropion, sertraline) and spiking experiments.

inconsistency.note: Where the same medicine was tested on several assays, results differed by assay, which the statement gives as the rule rather than a contradiction; the reviews disagree on one test (efavirenz and the Drug Screen Multi 5), which the statement reports.

indirectness.note: Second-hand. Each interference applies to the named test, and some tests have since changed (the clinical review notes that newer amphetamine assays no longer react to the Vicks inhaler); spiking experiments used concentrations not shown to occur in people's urine; the printed frequencies are shares of unconfirmed positives, not the chance that a person taking the medicine will screen positive.

imprecision.note: The few frequencies come from single chart reviews of 26 to 53 linked results with their totals unprinted, from groups of 6, 30 or 50 people, or from percentages without denominators.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; that reports of interference are likelier to be published than reports of none is counted under risk of bias.

large_effect.note: A descriptive claim is not upgraded for a large effect (METHODS §6.3).

grade.reasoning: Reports of false-positive screens are case reports, chart reviews, small dosing studies and laboratory experiments, seen here only through two narrative reviews: they start low (METHODS §6.3: claims seen only through reviews start from the design of the primary studies and are rated down for risk of bias and indirectness); risk of bias −1, indirectness −1 and imprecision −1 take the claim to very low, the floor. It rests only on narrative reviews, so it stays at draft and says that its figures are second-hand. The rule for test accuracy (METHODS §6.3) was considered and not applied: the claim says which medicines were reported to cause false positives on which tests, not how often a test reads right; the one accuracy-type comparison, efavirenz on one benzodiazepine test in 100 people with LC-MS/MS as the reference, is seen second-hand. Status replicated: separate reports by different teams, described in both reviews, agree that particular medicines can make particular screens read positive when confirmation finds no drug (efavirenz on cannabis screens in two studies, quinolone antibiotics on opiate screens in several); most single medicine-and-test pairs rest on one report, and the two reviews share sources, counted once. Nothing is phrased as advice on avoiding or passing a test; the clinical review's section on tampering with samples was not used.
